paras: The threatened lynching of Robert Garnes took place near Plain City and at Marysville, Ohio, on January 18, 1881, when crowds threatened to lynch Garnes, a Black farm hand arrested for a triple murder. Officers kept him from the crowds and slipped him into the Union County jail by a back entrance, and he was later indicted and convicted of second-degree murder.

On the night of Monday, January 17, Mrs. Ophelia Clark, an elderly Black woman who owned a farm near Plain City, her niece Maria Scott, and Charles Goode, a boy she had adopted, were beaten to death in their farmhouse. Garnes had worked or leased the farm until Mrs. Clark dismissed him, and according to the Chicago Tribune he had been rejected as a suitor by Maria Scott. He reported the killings at the Plain City telegraph office early the next morning, gave conflicting accounts under questioning, and was arrested after blood was found on his clothing. Papers also accused him of attempting to rape Maria Scott before the killings.

Hundreds of people visited the farm on January 18, and a Tribune dispatch said that "threats of lynching have been freely indulged in" and that a rope had been secured. The same dispatch said the threats would have been carried out "by the colored people of the vicinity had they been headed by a leader," but that the counsel of officers and of "the white people" held them back. For safety, officers took Garnes to Plain City.

That evening he was moved "by an out-of-the-way route" to Marysville, where a large crowd had gathered around the jail to await him. Officers brought him in by the back way about 9 o'clock and placed him in a cell, and the Tribune's Columbus correspondent wrote that had he been taken in the front way "he would have been lynched." A Marysville correspondent, writing the same night, said Garnes had been lodged "as quietly as possible" and that Sheriff Hobensack would stand by his prisoner "to the last."

No attempt on the jail was reported, and the Tribune said "the better part of the citizens" were glad Garnes was safely held for trial. A special grand jury at Marysville returned three indictments against him for first-degree murder. In May 1881 he was convicted at Marysville of murder in the second degree, which a dispatch said carried a life sentence. No report of arrests among the crowds appears in the coverage.

White papers covered the episode as a murder story, and the threat to Garnes appeared only as a detail within it. The first Columbus wire, which spelled his name "Garner" and called the dead woman Mrs. Matilda Scott, said nothing of lynching and ran under headlines such as "Beaten to Death by a Negro With a Hickory Club." Only the Chicago Tribune's special dispatches described the rope and the crowd at the jail, calling Garnes "the demon" and treating his guilt as all but settled.

Ohio weeklies reported the danger in a sentence each, the Somerset Press writing that "There is much fear that he will be lynched." Brief items in the Somerset Press, the Belmont Chronicle and the Shenandoah Herald later carried the indictments and the verdict. None of these papers condemned the crowds or commented on the threat.

Accounts of the murders differed on the victims' names and ages, the weapon, and how Garnes came under suspicion. The Marysville correspondent wrote that Garnes came home drunk and was arrested the next day without trying to escape, while the Somerset Press said the girl who found the bodies met him and he made off.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Robert Garnes
bases: A crowd threatened to lynch Garnes, a rope was secured, and a large crowd waited at the Marysville jail, but officers kept him in custody and no attempt on the jail was reported (A1, A4, A9).

The Chicago Tribune's Columbus dispatches (A1, A4) and a Marysville correspondent's letter (A9) independently report the lynching threats and Garnes being slipped into the jail, and the Somerset Press reports the fear of lynching (A8).

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune special dispatches
accounts.gist: Lynching threats were freely made at the scene, a rope was secured, and the colored people of the vicinity would have acted if led; Garnes was spirited to Plain City and then by a back route into the Marysville jail past a crowd that would have lynched him at the front door.

accounts.label: Marysville correspondent
accounts.gist: Garnes was brought to the jail after dark 'as quietly as possible'; threats of lynching were freely made and trouble might follow if anyone led it, but the sheriff would stand by his prisoner.

accounts.label: Columbus wire
accounts.gist: Reported the murders and Garnes's ('Garner's') arrest after he gave the alarm and told contradictory stories, without mentioning any lynching threat.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune reported the crowd at the jail without condemning it, called Garnes 'the demon' and 'the suspected and probable murderer', and noted that 'the better part of the citizens' were glad he was safely jailed for trial.
The Columbus wire, run under headlines such as 'Beaten to Death by a Negro With a Hickory Club', covered only the murders and the arrest.
Ohio weeklies reported the fear of lynching and the sheriff's resolve in a sentence each, then the indictments and verdict in brief items.
